Enuresis

1° vs 2° · mono- vs nonmonosymptomatic · urinalysis and exam · alarm vs desmopressinHas the urine been tested, and what has been tried, for how long?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Bedwetting at 5 or older, primary or secondary an examination and a urinalysis first; a stressor never replaces them
  • Daytime urgency, holding or hard stools nonmonosymptomatic: treat constipation and the daytime symptoms first
  • Normal workup motivational and behavioral therapy, then an alarm for a durable cure; desmopressin for a fast effect, usually from age 7
What it is

Repeated bedwetting, twice a week or more for at least 3 months, or with distress, in a child of 5 or older

Driver

Maturational in most primary cases: the child does not wake to a full bladder, and wetting comes in deep N3 sleep

Triggers

Family history (non-modifiable), the strongest risk factor; male sex (non-modifiable)

Constipation: a full rectum shrinks bladder capacity and makes the bladder muscle (detrusor) unstable

Obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy

A stressor (a new sibling, illness, a hospital stay)

Chain

Full bladder in deep sleep no waking wetting; usually outgrown

A new cause raises urine volume (diabetes, diabetes insipidus) or irritates the bladder (infection) wetting after 6 months dry

Insights

Tests only exclude a cause: enuresis itself is a clinical diagnosis, made once the urine and examination are normal

The alarm retrains waking, so its cure lasts; desmopressin, an antidiuretic hormone analog, only raises water reabsorption overnight, so wetting returns when it stops

2Urgent risks
Glucose in urineGlucose with or without ketones; thirst, weight loss

If the urine has glucose, choose serum glucose and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) for type 1 diabetes.

On desmopressinHeadache, vomiting or a seizure

If a child on desmopressin is unwell, choose hyponatremia: stop the drug; hypertonic saline for any neurologic symptom.

Spinal signsSacral dimple or tuft, abnormal gait or reflexes, new daytime accidents

If the spine or legs are abnormal, choose spinal MRI for a tethered cord.

StressorNew wetting after a separation or another stressor; behavior change

If a stressor is found, choose address it and screen for abuse, after the urinalysis.

3Differential
Bedwetting: the cause, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Primary monosymptomatic enuresis (primary nocturnal enuresis)Never dry for 6 months; bedwetting only; a parent wet the bedNormal examination and urinalysis
Nonmonosymptomatic enuresis (complex enuresis)
Daytime urgency, holding maneuvers, hard stoolsDaytime symptoms: constipation is treated first
Regression under stressDry 6 months or more, then wetting after a new sibling, a separation or a hospital stayNormal urinalysis first; the stressor alone never ends the workup
Urinary tract infection
New wetting with daytime accidents, often without dysuriaLeukocyte esterase and nitrites; culture
Type 1 diabetesThirst, weight loss, new wettingGlucose, with or without ketones, in the urine
Diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency or resistance)
Drinks through the night, large pale voidsVery low specific gravity; water deprivation test
Obstructive sleep apnea
Snoring, witnessed apneas, enlarged tonsils, mouth breathingPolysomnography
Posterior urethral valves
A boy with a weak stream or dribblingUS, then voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG)
Spinal dysraphism
Sacral dimple or tuft, abnormal gait or reflexes, back painSpinal MRI

4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Under 5 yearsBelow the diagnostic age; most resolveReassure
Camp or a sleepover soonA fast effect is neededDesmopressin
No better after 6 weeks of the alarmThe alarm is failingAdd or switch to desmopressin
Desmopressin with evening drinksWater retention, hyponatremiaNothing to drink from an hour before the dose until 8 hours after it

Pause point. The bait: blaming new wetting on divorce or a new sibling before a urinalysis. Test the urine first; then address the stressor.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria Enuresis – bedwetting on 2 or more nights a week for at least 3 months, or causing distress or impairment, from age 5 (or the same developmental level) · Primary – never dry for 6 months · Secondary – wetting again after 6 months or more dry · Nonmonosymptomatic – bedwetting plus urinary symptoms by day
6Severity
The type sets the plan
TypeCoursePlan
Under 5Normal at this ageReassure; no treatment
Primary monosymptomaticResolves about 14% a year Usually resolvesAbout 20% of children wet the bed at age 5 and 10% at age 10; about 14% a year resolve with no treatment, and the history and severity often follow the course of the affected family member.Behavioral therapy, then the ladder
NonmonosymptomaticComorbid causes, such as constipation, may contributeTreat constipation and daytime symptoms first; no alarm while bladder capacity is small
SecondaryA cause is likelierTreat the cause; with none found, the ladder
7Treatment
1

Behavioralmonosymptomatic, no cause found

Psychoeducation and behavioral training: reassurance, motivational therapy that rewards effort and routine, not dry nights

Void every 3 hours by day and before bed; stop drinks in the 1 to 2 hours before bed and drink well in the morning; treat constipation. Move on after 3 to 6 months without improvement, if the family is bothered.

2

Alarmbehavioral therapy fails; a motivated family

Bed-wetting alarm: the best long-term cure

Usually over age 6; may take up to 4 months; after 14 dry nights in a row it can stop, and it restarts on relapse.

AlarmThe child learns to link a full bladder with the alarm and wakes to void before wetting; the conditioning survives stopping the alarm, while desmopressin only lowers night urine output, so its effect does not.
3

Desmopressinpharmacotherapy, usually from age 7: nondrug therapy fails (the alarm after 6 weeks), or rapid improvement is desired

Oral desmopressin, the first-line drug; alone or with the alarm

Nothing to drink from an hour before the dose until 8 hours after it; not intranasal (hyponatremia); relapses more often after stopping.

4

Refractoryalarm and desmopressin both fail

Imipramine, rarely; urology referral

Oxybutynin only with desmopressin or imipramine, never alone.

ImipramineImipramine is second line for its worse side effects, rarely sudden death; an electrocardiogram (ECG) first, since a prolonged QT interval rules it out.
By situation
SituationChoose
Secondary enuresis with a causeTreat the cause
Desmopressin toxicity with neurologic symptomsStop the drug; hypertonic saline
Desmopressin toxicity, no symptomsStop the drug; strict water restriction
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Behavioral therapy, 3 to 6 monthsNo better and the family is bothered: alarm or desmopressin
Alarm, after 6 weeksNo better: add or switch to desmopressin
Alarm, 14 consecutive dry nightsConsider stopping; restart on relapse
Both failImipramine rarely, or urology referral
Practice
  1. 7-year-old boy wets the bed nightly has never had a dry night dry by day since age 4, no urgency or dribbling Nothing tried yet; three siblings were dry by age 3 Afebrile · examination normal · urinalysis normal · glucose 82 mg/dL → Education, reassurance and motivational therapy → primary and monosymptomatic with a normal workup and nothing tried: start on the first rung; desmopressin skips a tier, and 2 pm is the wrong hour (limit the evening, drink well in the morning); siblings dry by 3 is a parental comparison, not a clue, while a family history of enuresis would support a maturational cause
  2. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed nightly for 4 months was dry at night for 2 years no daytime urgency, dysuria or dribbling Otherwise healthy Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · examination normal → Secondary enuresis → 6 months or more of dryness before the wetting makes it secondary; a cause is sought, and the urinalysis comes first
  3. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for 3 weeks was dry at night for a year began after her parents separated Parents ask for counseling only Afebrile · BP 100/62 mm Hg · examination normal → Obtain the urinalysis first → a plausible stressor never replaces the urinalysis; one cheap test screens the organic causes, then address the stressor
  4. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for 2 weeks after a year dry drinking far more than usual tired, with 2 kg of weight loss No dysuria Afebrile · urinalysis: glucose 3+, ketones 1+, specific gravity 1.030 → New-onset diabetes mellitus → glucosuria with ketones in new wetting is type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise: serum glucose and HbA1c (hemoglobin A1c)
  5. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for a week after a year dry also has new daytime accidents No complaint of burning, and no stressor at home T 37.8 °C · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrites positive, no glucose → Urinary tract infection → a urinary infection can present as new wetting without dysuria in a child: urine culture, then treat
  6. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for a month after a year dry drinks water through the night large pale voids No dysuria Afebrile · urinalysis: specific gravity 1.002, no glucose, no leukocytes → Diabetes insipidus → a very low specific gravity in new wetting points to diabetes insipidus: a water deprivation test, then the desmopressin response
  7. 6-year-old girl wets the bed nightly has daytime urgency and squats on her heel to hold urine stools hard, every 4 days Never dry at night Afebrile · examination: stool palpable in the left lower quadrant → Nonmonosymptomatic enuresis → daytime symptoms make it nonmonosymptomatic: bladder diary, and treat the constipation first, which is often curative
  8. 7-year-old girl still wets the bed most nights 8 months of reward charts and a voiding routine family distressed and keen to keep trying Dry by day; no constipation Afebrile · examination and urinalysis normal → Enuresis alarm → tier 1 has failed past 3 to 6 months in a bothered, motivated family: the alarm gives the most durable cure
  9. 7-year-old girl who has never been dry at night goes to sleepaway camp next week 4 months of reward charts have helped only a little Dry by day; no constipation; parents want a quick fix Afebrile · examination and urinalysis normal → Desmopressin → event-driven beats durable: desmopressin works within days; the alarm needs weeks; oxybutynin is not used alone
  10. 7-year-old girl taking desmopressin for wetting the bed has headache and vomiting had a seizure an hour ago drank several cups of juice at a party tonight Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg · serum sodium pending → Hyponatremia → desmopressin is an ADH (antidiuretic hormone) analog; free-water retention gives both its effect and its hyponatremic seizures: stop it; a seizure needs hypertonic saline
  11. 7-year-old boy wets the bed nightly and dribbles by day weak urinary stream dribbling after voiding Never dry at night; no constipation or urgency Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg · examination otherwise normal → Posterior urethral valves → a weak stream or dribbling in a boy is posterior urethral valves until proven otherwise: renal ultrasound and VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram)
  12. 6-year-old girl wets the bed nightly and now has daytime accidents a tuft of hair over the sacrum brisk lower-extremity reflexes Dry by day from age 3 until this year; no constipation Afebrile · BP 100/60 mm Hg · urinalysis normal → Spinal MRI → a sacral tuft with abnormal neurology is spinal dysraphism: spinal MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), not reassurance
  13. 4-year-old boy wets the bed most nights dry during the day, no urgency or constipation Parents are worried because his cousin was dry at 3 and ask about medicine Afebrile · growth normal · examination normal → Reassurance → enuresis is not diagnosed before age 5: reassure, since many children become dry without treatment
Pairs with Polyuria covers the next step once a very low specific gravity points to diabetes insipidus: the water deprivation test, what its result means, and the one child in whom it must not be done. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule

Set the tier by what has been done and for how long: a normal workup means no further testing, and no treatment yet means no escalation. Pick the lowest rung not yet exhausted.
